summaries.beginner: Some eye cells that help set our body clock also react to blue light in a special “off” way in primates. By tracing monkey retinal wiring, the authors found a previously unknown cell that flips a blue-on signal into that blue-off response.
summaries.intermediate: Patterson et al. (Current Biology, 2020) reconstruct macaque blue-cone circuitry with serial EM. They discover an amacrine cell driven exclusively by S-ON bipolar cells that inhibits ipRGCs, accounting for the S-OFF response. They present this as the missing element of an evolutionarily ancient spectral circuit for non-image-forming vision.
summaries.advanced: Circuit identity is EM-based in macaque; primate-to-human inference is explicit but untested. “Exclusive” S-ON input and “highly selective” ipRGC synapses are claims from the reconstructed volume. Functional blue-OFF physiology is the explanandum from prior work, tied here to the new cell’s inhibitory synapses.

plain_language_summary: Some eye cells that help set our body clock also react to blue light in a special “off” way in primates. By tracing monkey retinal wiring, the authors found a previously unknown cell that flips a blue-on signal into that blue-off response.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous-system organization spans synapse placement, neuron shape, circuits, and brain regions; C. elegans is small enough that these scales can be combined in one model of the nerve ring.
ocar.challenge: No complete structure–function model had integrated volumetric reconstructions with chemical and gap-junction connectomes of the main neuropil.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen (bioRxiv, 2020) integrate volumetric reconstructions from two animals with synaptic and gap-junction connectomes of the nerve ring.
ocar.resolution: They describe five functional bundles that spatially constrain synapses; a precisely wired core embedded in variable connectivity, with a proposed core reference connectome; and an architecture they liken to a modular residual network for sensory integration and brain-wide coordination.
ocar.future_work: The core-versus-variable split comes from two animals; more individuals would test how stable the reference core is.

summaries.beginner: Researchers rebuilt the main nerve bundle of the worm in 3D, not just as a list of connections. They found the wires are grouped into bundles, and that some connections are very consistent while others vary between animals.
summaries.intermediate: Brittin et al. (bioRxiv, 2020) integrate two C. elegans volumetric reconstructions with chemical and gap-junction connectomes of the nerve ring. Previously treated as a packed axon tract, the ring contains five functional bundles that constrain synapses. Connectivity is not invariant: a precisely wired core sits in a variable background. They analogize the architecture to a modular residual network.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. n=2 animals limits the core/variable partition. Residual-network language is a conceptual mapping, not a trained ResNet. Gap-junction versus chemical contributions to “modules” should be read as model interpretation of the combined graphs.

plain_language_summary: Researchers rebuilt the main nerve bundle of the worm in 3D, not just as a list of connections. They found the wires are grouped into bundles, and that some connections are very consistent while others vary between animals.

ocar.opportunity: Human high acuity depends on a foveal private line: cone → midget bipolar → midget ganglion cell. How that one-to-one wiring arises in development is unknown.
ocar.challenge: It could be specified early with extreme precision or emerge slowly as foveal architecture and sensitivity mature.
ocar.action: Zhang et al. (Neuron, 2020) reconstruct midget circuitry in fetal human fovea by serial electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: The private line is sculpted by synaptic remodeling from early fetal life: midget bipolar cells contact a single cone by mid-gestation, while bipolar–ganglion connectivity refines over a longer period.
ocar.future_work: The study maps fetal stages available in the EM series; later postnatal refinement of human foveal midget circuits is outside this dataset.

summaries.beginner: Sharp human vision starts with a private pathway from each cone in the center of the eye to its own outgoing cell. By looking at fetal human retinas with electron microscopy, this team found that this private wiring is carved out by remodeling connections, not finished in one early step.
summaries.intermediate: Zhang et al. (Neuron, 2020) use serial EM to reconstruct developing human foveal midget circuits. They find the private-line architecture is shaped by synaptic remodeling: bipolar cells contact a single cone by mid-gestation, whereas bipolar-to-ganglion contacts refine more slowly. This favors gradual emergence over instantaneous early specification.
summaries.advanced: Fetal EM is a series of snapshots, not longitudinal imaging of the same cells. “Mid-gestation” is the bipolar-to-cone milestone stated; exact gestational ages are not in the abstract. Catalog organism tags saying mouse conflict with the human fetal material.

plain_language_summary: Sharp human vision starts with a private pathway from each cone in the center of the eye to its own outgoing cell. By looking at fetal human retinas with electron microscopy, this team found that this private wiring is carved out by remodeling connections, not finished in one early step.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes invite linking structure to function, but standard graph metrics may ignore how networks actually spike to shared inputs.
ocar.challenge: Which architectural features predict similar stimulus-evoked spike patterns is unclear.
ocar.action: Haber and Schneidman (bioRxiv, 2020) simulate networks, measure functional similarity as spike-pattern similitude to the same stimuli, learn a metric from synaptic differences, and search for sparse predictors.
ocar.resolution: Common graph-theory metrics convey little about response similarity. A learned functional metric predicts similarity on novel networks across many stimuli. A sparse feature set—each neuron’s total synaptic input and total synaptic output—predicts functional similarity for networks of up to 100 cells.
ocar.future_work: The 100-cell simulated regime and homeostatic interpretation are the stated scope; mapping the same features onto biological connectomes is suggested by the homeostasis remark, not shown.

summaries.beginner: Two brain circuits can look similar as stick-figure graphs and still behave differently. In computer-simulated networks, this study found that simple totals—how much input and output each cell has—predict whether two networks will fire in similar patterns.
summaries.intermediate: Haber and Schneidman (bioRxiv, 2020) define functional similarity of simulated networks by spike-pattern likeness under identical stimuli. Standard graph metrics predict this poorly. A learned synaptic-difference metric generalizes to new networks, and the sums of each neuron’s synaptic in-weights and out-weights suffice up to 100 cells, consistent with homeostatic design ideas.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint on simulated networks, not reconstructed tissue. “Up to 100 cells” is an explicit scale limit. Functional similarity is stimulus-set dependent even though they report a wide range. Biological confirmation is not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Two brain circuits can look similar as stick-figure graphs and still behave differently. In computer-simulated networks, this study found that simple totals—how much input and output each cell has—predict whether two networks will fire in similar patterns.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse connectomes have usually been parcellated into regions, which can hide fine network structure. A voxel-level directed map would link mesoscale anatomy to macroscale function.
ocar.challenge: Regional partitions limit spatial resolution and may conceal hubs, communities, and gradients.
ocar.action: Coletta et al. (bioRxiv / Science Advances DOI in metadata, 2020) describe the directed mouse connectome at voxel resolution without regional partitioning.
ocar.resolution: Hubs split into neural sinks and sources along a hierarchy; structural communities reconstitute known fMRI networks; neuromodulatory nuclei look like orchestrators of inter-modular communication. Two cortical gradients resemble primate unimodal–transmodal and sensorimotor axes and relate to intralaminar connectivity and dynamic fMRI states.
ocar.future_work: Voxel-level maps invite intervention targeting; the abstract presents opportunities rather than stimulation experiments.

summaries.beginner: Most mouse brain-connection maps color large regions as single units. This study instead looks voxel by voxel and finds a hierarchy of sending versus receiving hubs, communities that match known brain-wide activity networks, and two large spatial trends like those in primates.
summaries.intermediate: Coletta et al. (2020; journal field bioRxiv) analyze a directed mouse connectome at voxel resolution. Integrative hubs separate into sinks and sources along a hierarchical axis. Structural communities spatially match previously described mouse fMRI networks, and neuromodulatory nuclei appear positioned to orchestrate inter-modular communicability. Two superimposed cortical gradients recall primate unimodal–transmodal and sensorimotor axes.
summaries.advanced: This is mesoscale (tracer-based) connectivity at voxel resolution, not synaptic EM. Journal metadata say bioRxiv while the DOI is Science Advances. Gradient interpretations relating to fMRI states are structure–function associations. Parcellation-free analysis still depends on registration and tracer-direction accuracy.

plain_language_summary: Most mouse brain-connection maps color large regions as single units. This study instead looks voxel by voxel and finds a hierarchy of sending versus receiving hubs, communities that match known brain-wide activity networks, and two large spatial trends like those in primates.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit wiring is often inferred from multi-neuron activity when anatomy cannot be measured. Knowing when that inference is systematically wrong is essential.
ocar.challenge: Even sophisticated methods with unlimited data from every cell can fail if the inference model does not match true dynamics—especially in strongly recurrent networks with correlated neurons.
ocar.action: Das and Fiete (Nature Neuroscience, 2020) analyze connectivity inference in strongly recurrent circuits and consider driving networks far from equilibrium with a simple suppressive drive.
ocar.resolution: Inferred diagrams are biased toward synapses between unconnected but highly correlated neurons because of failed “explaining away.” Activity-based estimates need special caution in strongly connected nets; non-equilibrium suppression may reduce bias.
ocar.future_work: The proposed remedy is to infer from circuits pushed out of equilibrium; empirical recipes for doing that in vivo are only sketched at the abstract level.

summaries.beginner: People often try to guess which brain cells are wired together just from watching them fire. This paper shows that in tightly looping circuits those guesses can systematically invent connections between cells that merely fire together, even if you record every cell forever.
summaries.intermediate: Das and Fiete (Nature Neuroscience, 2020) show that connectivity inferred from activity in strongly recurrent networks is biased toward false edges between correlated but unconnected neurons. The bias survives sophisticated methods and complete, unlimited recordings when the generative model is misspecified. They suggest inference on activity far from equilibrium, using a low-dimensional suppressive drive, as a possible fix.
summaries.advanced: The result is a theoretical/simulation demonstration of systematic bias, not a particular experimental dataset. Model mismatch is described as inevitable in the real world. The non-equilibrium remedy is proposed, not proven as a universal protocol. Strong recurrence and high correlation are the danger regime they highlight.

plain_language_summary: People often try to guess which brain cells are wired together just from watching them fire. This paper shows that in tightly looping circuits those guesses can systematically invent connections between cells that merely fire together, even if you record every cell forever.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila larva offers genetic tractability, robust learning assays, single-cell manipulation, and an emerging complete CNS synaptic connectome for studying memory in a ~10,000-neuron brain.
ocar.challenge: Even the much-studied mushroom body still hid more than half of its connection classes until the larval connectome was examined, so function cannot be read from textbook motifs alone.
ocar.action: Thum and Gerber (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2019) review larval mushroom-body connectomics together with dopamine-timing experiments and molecularly dissociable memory phases.
ocar.resolution: The connectome revealed circuitry that integrates sensory input, valence, and output within and across hemispheres. Activating individual dopaminergic mushroom-body input neurons can reward or punish an odor depending on timing, and larvae form short-term, long-term, and amnesia-resistant memories that are molecularly separable.
ocar.future_work: They present the larval mushroom body as a system for a nuanced account of molecular function in a behaviorally meaningful memory network; that program is ongoing.

summaries.beginner: Young fruit flies can learn, and their memory center is simple enough to map cell by cell. This review explains how that map showed many previously missed connection types and how the timing of dopamine can make the same pathway feel rewarding or punishing.
summaries.intermediate: Thum and Gerber (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2019) review the larval Drosophila mushroom body as a memory network. Connectomics showed that more than half of mushroom-body connection classes had been overlooked, and it revealed intra- and inter-hemispheric integration of sensory, valence, and output neurons. Individual dopaminergic inputs can reward or punish depending on relative timing, and larvae form molecularly dissociable short-term, long-term, and amnesia-resistant memories.
summaries.advanced: This is a review of connectome plus behavior/molecular work, not a primary EM paper. “More than half of connection classes” is a connectome finding they highlight. Timing-dependent valence and memory phases are attributed to prior experiments synthesized here. Completeness claims depend on the larval CNS volume then available.

plain_language_summary: Young fruit flies can learn, and their memory center is simple enough to map cell by cell. This review explains how that map showed many previously missed connection types and how the timing of dopamine can make the same pathway feel rewarding or punishing.

ocar.opportunity: Structural and functional connectomes span nanometer synapses to centimeter organs and sub-millisecond events to years of behavior, so imaging must cover those scales.
ocar.challenge: No single optical tool simultaneously offers speed, resolution, contrast, depth, large volume, and molecular specificity.
ocar.action: Gogoi, Keiser, Kao, and Chiang (2019 book chapter) review optical modalities aimed at high-throughput brain imaging and the obstacles to imaging the connectome.
ocar.resolution: They survey recent optical advances that extract new circuit insight while cataloging remaining challenges of scale and specificity.
ocar.future_work: The chapter frames unsolved trade-offs among speed, resolution, depth, and molecular contrast as the agenda for later tools.

summaries.beginner: Brains have to be pictured from tiny synapses up to the whole organ, and from split-second signals up to long-term behavior. This chapter reviews light-based cameras and microscopes that try to do that, and the problems that remain.
summaries.intermediate: Gogoi et al. (2019 book chapter; no journal in the record) review multiscale, multimodal optical imaging for connectomics. They stress that neural structure spans nanometers to centimeters and function spans sub-milliseconds to years, so ideal tools need speed, resolution, contrast, depth, volume, and molecular specificity. The chapter surveys high-throughput optical methods and remaining obstacles.
summaries.advanced: This is a review chapter, not a new instrument paper. No quantitative bake-off is in the abstract. Optical methods still generally lack EM’s synapse certainty; the chapter is about light-microscopy connectomics, not volume EM.

plain_language_summary: Brains have to be pictured from tiny synapses up to the whole organ, and from split-second signals up to long-term behavior. This chapter reviews light-based cameras and microscopes that try to do that, and the problems that remain.

ocar.opportunity: Brain atlases and connectomics need whole-brain maps at single-neuron resolution with precise spatial coordinates tied to genome, proteome, and other -omes—what the authors call brainsmatics.
ocar.challenge: Among imaging methods, only optical imaging currently offers a path to whole-brain connectomes at consistent single-neuron resolution, but tracing and surveying strategies are still evolving.
ocar.action: Shi, Guan, Chen, and Luo (Photonics, 2019) review optical imaging’s role in brainsmatics, focusing on tracing and surveying, and they call for a global interdisciplinary community.
ocar.resolution: They position optical imaging as the leading approach for brain-wide spatial informatics and sketch development objectives for the field.
ocar.future_work: They explicitly invite neuroscientists, engineers, chemists, clinicians, and others to contribute; optical methods would in turn benefit from that community.

summaries.beginner: To understand a whole brain, scientists need maps that keep every cell’s location and its connections. This review argues that light microscopy is the best current way to do that at the scale of single neurons across an entire brain, and it asks many fields to help.
summaries.intermediate: Shi et al. (Photonics, 2019) coin and review “brainsmatics”: brain-wide spatial informatics linking connectome, genome, proteome, transcriptome, and metabolome to precise positions. They argue optical imaging is the most suitable route to whole-brain connectomes at consistent single-neuron resolution, emphasizing tracing and surveying. The article is a field call, not a new microscope.
summaries.advanced: “Most appropriate” is a position, not a benchmark versus EM or MRI. Single-neuron optical resolution is not synaptic ultrastructure. Brainsmatics is a proposed umbrella, not a completed atlas.

plain_language_summary: To understand a whole brain, scientists need maps that keep every cell’s location and its connections. This review argues that light microscopy is the best current way to do that at the scale of single neurons across an entire brain, and it asks many fields to help.

ocar.opportunity: Serial block-face SEM, introduced in 2004, made large-scale 3D ultrastructure more reliable and available than classic serial-section TEM or tomography for cellular-scale volumes.
ocar.challenge: Earlier 3DEM on a cellular scale was hampered by the difficulty of cutting and reconstructing thousands of sections.
ocar.action: Smith and Starborg (Tissue & Cell, 2019) review biological SBFSEM from a technical standpoint, with cellular applications and downstream image analysis, including connectomics.
ocar.resolution: They describe SBFSEM as resolving membranes and small vesicles while retaining a large field of view, and they survey applications in connectomics, cell biology, and matrix biology.
ocar.future_work: The review points to analysis of large SBFSEM volumes as a continuing bottleneck alongside acquisition.

summaries.beginner: A 3D electron-microscope method that slices and images a sample inside the microscope has made it much easier to see cells in volume. This review explains how that method works and where it has been used, including brain wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Smith and Starborg (Tissue & Cell, 2019) review serial block-face SEM (SBFSEM) as a 3DEM technique dating to 2004. They contrast it with serial-section TEM and electron tomography, note resolution sufficient for membranes and small vesicles with large fields of view, and survey applications including connectomics plus image-analysis workflows. The article is a methods review.
summaries.advanced: SBFSEM’s z-resolution and charging/cutting artifacts are known trade-offs not quantified here. “2004” is the development date they cite. Connectomics is one application among several; this is not a new circuit map.

plain_language_summary: A 3D electron-microscope method that slices and images a sample inside the microscope has made it much easier to see cells in volume. This review explains how that method works and where it has been used, including brain wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Automated Tape-Collecting Ultramicrotomy (ATUM) can gather thousands of serial sections for SEM, enabling large connectomic volumes including mouse brain.
ocar.challenge: Handling the microtome, tape, post-treatment, mapping, imaging, and alignment is a specialized craft that needs a written protocol.
ocar.action: Baena, Schalek, Lichtman, and Terasaki (Methods in Cell Biology, 2019) describe preparing a block, using ATUM, preparing tape, treating sections, and mapping/imaging/aligning serial sections.
ocar.resolution: They present ATUM as suitable both for large-scale mouse-brain connectomics and for smaller studies of tissues, cells, and organisms.
ocar.future_work: The chapter is a how-to; successful use still depends on local ultramicrotomy skill and SEM capacity.

summaries.beginner: One way to build a giant 3D electron-microscope map is to catch thousands of ultra-thin slices on tape and then photograph them. This chapter explains, step by step, how to do that.
summaries.intermediate: Baena et al. (Methods in Cell Biology, 2019) detail Automated Tape-Collecting Ultramicrotome (ATUM) serial-section EM. They cover block preparation, ATUM handling, tape, post-treatment, and mapping, imaging, and alignment of sections. They note use in large-scale mouse-brain connectomics and in smaller projects. The article is a methods chapter.
summaries.advanced: ATUM collects sections for SEM; it does not itself segment neurons. Throughput and section loss rates are not in the abstract. Mouse-brain connectomics is cited as a use case, not a dataset released here.

plain_language_summary: One way to build a giant 3D electron-microscope map is to catch thousands of ultra-thin slices on tape and then photograph them. This chapter explains, step by step, how to do that.

ocar.opportunity: Rabbit retina has many ganglion-cell types; Class IV sparsely branched SB3 cells need a synaptic census to explain their function.
ocar.challenge: Identifying which bipolar and amacrine types contact a sparse, sublamina-a ramifying cell requires EM reconstruction.
ocar.action: Bordt et al. (Visual Neuroscience, 2019) partially reconstruct an SB3 cell in an automated TEM rabbit retinal connectome and catalog bipolar and amacrine inputs.
ocar.resolution: The cell was always postsynaptic, received 29% of input from multiple presumed OFF bipolars (typically one synapse each, infrequent dyad reciprocals), and most amacrine input from GABAergic axons/dendrites likely providing extra-classical inhibition, with little crossover from narrow-field ON amacrines.
ocar.future_work: Partial reconstruction of one cell leaves type-wide variability and physiology of the SB3 receptive field for later work.

summaries.beginner: Researchers traced one uncommon type of rabbit retinal ganglion cell in a 3D electron-microscope map. About a third of its incoming connections came from several kinds of OFF bipolar cells, and most of the rest came from inhibitory amacrine cells, including some that likely bring information from outside the cell’s classic viewing area.
summaries.intermediate: Bordt et al. (Visual Neuroscience, 2019) reconstruct a sparsely branched Class IV (SB3) ganglion cell in a rabbit ATEM connectome. Dendrites in sublamina a were exclusively postsynaptic. Bipolar cells supplied 29% of input from multiple presumed OFF types, usually one synapse per bipolar; GABAergic wide-field amacrine axons and dendrites supplied most of the rest. Narrow-field ON amacrine crossover inhibition was apparently absent.
summaries.advanced: 29% bipolar input is from one partially reconstructed cell. Bipolar types are “presumed OFF.” Extra-classical inhibition is inferred from GABAergic wide-field morphology, not from receptive-field mapping of this cell. Catalog dataset tags for mouse retina do not match rabbit material.

plain_language_summary: Researchers traced one uncommon type of rabbit retinal ganglion cell in a 3D electron-microscope map. About a third of its incoming connections came from several kinds of OFF bipolar cells, and most of the rest came from inhibitory amacrine cells, including some that likely bring information from outside the cell’s classic viewing area.

ocar.opportunity: ON parasol ganglion cells are a major primate retinal output, but the amacrine contribution to their circuit, especially from wide-field cells, is poorly specified.
ocar.challenge: Wide-field GABAergic amacrines with long, straight processes are hard to reconstruct and to assign to named types.
ocar.action: Patterson et al. (Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2019) reconstruct six neighboring ON parasol cells in a central macaque SBF-SEM connectome and analyze their inputs.
ocar.resolution: On average, 21% of input was bipolar and 17% was wide-field amacrine. Two wide-field types were identified: semilunar type 2 (polyaxonal, electrically coupled to ON parasols) and wiry type 2 (motion-sensitive). These inputs likely increase sensitivity to rapidly changing stimuli outside classical receptive fields.
ocar.future_work: Six neighboring cells in central macaque constrain eccentricity and sample size; other amacrine classes remain to be fully typed in the volume.

summaries.beginner: Parasol cells are important outgoing cells in monkey retinas. A 3D wiring map of six neighboring ON parasol cells showed that a sizable share of their incoming connections come from far-reaching inhibitory cells, which may help them notice motion outside their usual patch of the world.
summaries.intermediate: Patterson et al. (Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2019) reconstruct six neighboring macaque ON parasol cells. Mean input was 21% bipolar and 17% wide-field amacrine. Wide-field types include semilunar type 2, a polyaxonal cell coupled to ON parasols, and wiry type 2, known to be motion-sensitive. The authors suggest these inputs heighten sensitivity to rapidly changing extra-classical stimuli.
summaries.advanced: Percentages are averages over six cells in central retina. “Likely” extra-classical effects are inferred from amacrine anatomy and prior physiology, not from recording these reconstructed cells. Remaining amacrine input beyond 17% wide-field is not fully broken down in the abstract. Catalog mouse-retina tags do not match macaque.

plain_language_summary: Parasol cells are important outgoing cells in monkey retinas. A 3D wiring map of six neighboring ON parasol cells showed that a sizable share of their incoming connections come from far-reaching inhibitory cells, which may help them notice motion outside their usual patch of the world.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic reconstruction of neural circuits from EM needs membrane segmentation that survives anisotropic, thick, low-quality imagery.
ocar.challenge: Connectome segmentation is hard because neurons have both filament-like and blob-like membranes and confusing intracellular texture, and labels are scarce.
ocar.action: Chen, Zhu, Lu, and Luo (Symmetry, 2018) propose ADDN: a conditional GAN with a densely dilated network segmentor, trained with adversarial plus dice loss.
ocar.resolution: They report more accurate boundaries, reduced blurry boundary maps, state-of-the-art performance, and lower computation on ISBI 2012 EM and mouse piriform cortex datasets.
ocar.future_work: SOTA is claimed on those two datasets; generalization to newer large fly or mammalian volumes is not shown.

summaries.beginner: Computers must outline cell membranes in messy electron-microscope pictures before scientists can rebuild circuits. This paper uses two networks that compete with each other to draw sharper outlines, and it reports strong results on two public datasets.
summaries.intermediate: Chen et al. (Symmetry, 2018) introduce ADDN, a conditional GAN whose segmentor is a densely dilated network for connectome membrane segmentation. Adversarial loss is combined with dice loss. They claim state-of-the-art accuracy with less computation on ISBI 2012 and mouse piriform cortex EM, and less blurry boundary maps.
summaries.advanced: “State-of-the-art” is the authors’ claim; numeric scores are not in the abstract. cGANs can be unstable; they do not discuss failure modes here. ISBI 2012 is a small, saturated benchmark relative to modern petascale volumes. Anisotropic EM remains the motivating difficulty.

plain_language_summary: Computers must outline cell membranes in messy electron-microscope pictures before scientists can rebuild circuits. This paper uses two networks that compete with each other to draw sharper outlines, and it reports strong results on two public datasets.

ocar.opportunity: The insect central complex is a conserved, stereotyped region implicated in many behaviors and often modeled from light-microscopy overlap.
ocar.challenge: Overlap is not connectivity; functional synapses between cell types need to be measured.
ocar.action: Franconville, Beron, and Jayaraman (eLife, 2018) test 70 presynaptic–postsynaptic cell-type pairs in Drosophila with simultaneous optogenetic stimulation, calcium imaging, and pharmacology.
ocar.resolution: They find numerous inputs to the central complex but few output channels, sparser connectivity than light-microscopy overlap suggested, and a potentially critical class of bottleneck interneurons. Data are shared on an interactive website.
ocar.future_work: The functional matrix is at cell-type resolution, not synapse counts; combining it with later EM connectomes is a natural sequel they enable by sharing data.

summaries.beginner: A deep part of the fly brain called the central complex helps with navigation and other behaviors. Instead of guessing connections from overlapping cell shapes, this team stimulated one cell type at a time and watched which others responded, finding fewer links than pictures had suggested.
summaries.intermediate: Franconville, Beron, and Jayaraman (eLife, 2018) build a cell-type-resolution functional connectome of the Drosophila central complex. Testing 70 pre-to-post pairs with optogenetics, calcium imaging, and pharmacology, they report many input pathways, few output channels, and sparser recurrence than expected from light-microscopy overlap, highlighting bottleneck interneurons. Data are provided for interactive exploration.
summaries.advanced: Functional connectivity can miss weak or highly conditional synapses and can include indirect paths despite pharmacology. Seventy pairs is a large but not exhaustive matrix. “Sparser than anticipated from overlap” is the key methodological moral. Bottleneck interneurons are highlighted as potentially critical, not fully proven as computational chokepoints.

plain_language_summary: A deep part of the fly brain called the central complex helps with navigation and other behaviors. Instead of guessing connections from overlapping cell shapes, this team stimulated one cell type at a time and watched which others responded, finding fewer links than pictures had suggested.

ocar.opportunity: Primate midget ganglion cells are the classic L-versus-M color substrate; whether some OFF midgets also carry S-cone signals, and how that changes color tuning, was unclear.
ocar.challenge: Physiology suggested sparse S input to some OFF midgets, but an S-cone → OFF midget bipolar → OFF midget ganglion anatomical path remained ambiguous.
ocar.action: Wool, Packer, Zaidi, and Dacey (Journal of Neuroscience, 2018) use serial block-face EM in macaque parafovea plus patch recordings of OFF midgets with mixed L, M, and S input.
ocar.resolution: Every parafoveal S cone synapsed mainly onto a single OFF midget bipolar that privately contacted an OFF midget ganglion cell. S-OFF midgets show an S-cone spatial signature but heterogeneous color tuning from variable L, M, and S weights, expanding color coding beyond cardinal L-versus-M and S-versus-L+M axes.
ocar.future_work: Anatomy is parafoveal; physiology is near peripheral—whether the private-line S-OFF path persists at all eccentricities is not settled in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Color vision in primates is often described as red-versus-green and blue-versus-yellow. This study shows that some “green-off” outgoing cells in the monkey eye also get a private blue-cone input, so their color preferences can sit off those two classic axes.
summaries.intermediate: Wool et al. (Journal of Neuroscience, 2018) combine macaque SBF-SEM with electrophysiology. In parafovea, each S cone principally synapses on one OFF midget bipolar with a private-line connection to an OFF midget ganglion cell. Near-peripheral S-OFF midgets have mixed L, M, and S weights and noncardinal color tuning despite a recognizable S spatial signature.
summaries.advanced: EM and physiology are at different eccentricities (parafovea vs near periphery). “Every S cone” is a claim about the reconstructed parafoveal volume. Heterogeneous 3D color tuning is physiological, not a full population census. Catalog mouse-retina tags do not match macaque.

plain_language_summary: Color vision in primates is often described as red-versus-green and blue-versus-yellow. This study shows that some “green-off” outgoing cells in the monkey eye also get a private blue-cone input, so their color preferences can sit off those two classic axes.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience imaging stacks often reach gigabytes per experiment; automated tracing could complete circuits, but learning-based methods are error-prone and slow.
ocar.challenge: Supervised segmenters need training data and may not transfer across EM, confocal reflectance, and X-ray microtomography.
ocar.action: Shahbazi et al. (bioRxiv, 2018) introduce FLoRIN, a fast learning-free sparse segmentation and reconstruction pipeline using structure-specific context, tested on sSEM, SCoRe, and synchrotron µCT mouse volumes.
ocar.resolution: They report reconstructions of sufficient quality for preliminary biology, robustness to noise and artifacts, and speed up to several orders of magnitude faster than existing supervised methods.
ocar.future_work: “Preliminary biological study” quality is the claim; dense synapse-complete tracing is not the stated product.

summaries.beginner: Brain-imaging experiments can produce huge piles of pictures, and teaching a computer to trace cells usually requires lots of hand-labeled examples. This team built a faster tracer that does not need that training and works on several kinds of microscopes.
summaries.intermediate: Shahbazi et al. (bioRxiv, 2018) present FLoRIN, a learning-free sparse segmentation and reconstruction method for neural volumes. It uses structure-specific contextual cues and is tested on serial-section SEM, spectral confocal reflectance, and synchrotron X-ray microtomography in mouse. They claim much higher speed than supervised methods and robustness to noise, with reconstructions usable for preliminary biology.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Speed “up to several orders of magnitude” has no numeric table in the abstract. Learning-free methods can still embed strong heuristics that fail on new stains. Sparse tracing is not a dense EM connectome. Quality is described as sufficient for preliminary study, not proofread ground truth.

plain_language_summary: Brain-imaging experiments can produce huge piles of pictures, and teaching a computer to trace cells usually requires lots of hand-labeled examples. This team built a faster tracer that does not need that training and works on several kinds of microscopes.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans remains the only organism with a complete synaptic nervous-system map (1986), now joined by extrasynaptic neuropeptide and monoamine maps.
ocar.challenge: Understanding how wired synapses interact with wireless neuromodulation to produce behavior requires combining perturbations, imaging, models, and quantification.
ocar.action: DiLoreto, Chute, Bryce, and Srinivasan (2018 preprint) review whole-brain imaging, optogenetics, sonogenetics, and mutant analysis of local and global C. elegans circuits.
ocar.resolution: They argue that a complete organism-level picture needs experimental datasets plus biophysical modeling and behavioral quantification, including extrasynaptic networks that modulate the synaptic connectome.
ocar.future_work: The review sets an agenda for integrating extrasynaptic maps with the synaptic connectome rather than delivering that integration.

summaries.beginner: The worm C. elegans is still the only animal with a complete map of its chemical synapses, and researchers have now also mapped some of its slower chemical broadcast systems. This review discusses new tools for turning cells on and off and for watching the whole brain, aiming at a fuller picture of how the worm thinks and acts.
summaries.intermediate: DiLoreto et al. (2018 preprint; no journal in the record) review functional connectomics in C. elegans, from the 1986 synaptic map through extrasynaptic neuropeptide and monoamine connectomes. They survey whole-brain imaging, optogenetics, sonogenetics, and mutants for perturbing local and global circuits. They argue that experiments must be combined with biophysical models and behavioral quantification.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/preprint, not new wiring data. Sonogenetics and whole-brain imaging capabilities are cited at a high level. Completeness of extrasynaptic maps is as of 2018. No primary numbers appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: The worm C. elegans is still the only animal with a complete map of its chemical synapses, and researchers have now also mapped some of its slower chemical broadcast systems. This review discusses new tools for turning cells on and off and for watching the whole brain, aiming at a fuller picture of how the worm thinks and acts.

ocar.opportunity: Graph spectral embeddings can reveal distributed structure not visible node-wise; C. elegans is a testbed with known cell classes.
ocar.challenge: Standard Laplacian embeddings do not let the analyst focus on a chosen cell class or trade global versus local effects via node importance weights.
ocar.action: Petrović et al. (Network Neuroscience, 2018) define a guided spectral embedding that jointly maximizes energy concentration and minimizes a modified embedded distance given node weights, then apply it to the C. elegans structural connectome.
ocar.resolution: The two goals are intrinsically opposite, yielding a stable decomposition. Focusing on sensory, inter-, or motor neurons yields more biological insight than Laplacian embedding, including somatic position and low- versus high-order processing involvement, matching known function and importance.
ocar.future_work: The method is demonstrated on C. elegans; applying guided embedding to larger connectomes is not shown.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram can be redrawn so that hidden patterns pop out, like a map projection. This paper adds a way to highlight chosen cell types in the worm’s wiring and finds splits that match where cells sit in the body and what jobs they do.
summaries.intermediate: Petrović et al. (Network Neuroscience, 2018) introduce guided graph spectral embedding, combining energy concentration with a weighted embedded-distance objective. On the C. elegans structural connectome, importance weighting tunes global versus local focus. Guided embeddings for sensory, inter-, and motor neurons recover biological distinctions (somatic position, processing order) better than Laplacian embedding.
summaries.advanced: “More biological insights” is qualitative. Stability is argued from opposing objectives, not from a large ablation in the abstract. Structural connectome version (chemical vs gap junction) is not specified here. Spectral methods depend on how the adjacency is weighted.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram can be redrawn so that hidden patterns pop out, like a map projection. This paper adds a way to highlight chosen cell types in the worm’s wiring and finds splits that match where cells sit in the body and what jobs they do.

ocar.opportunity: Mesoscale connectomes describe connections among neuronal types across regions and are the middle layer between MRI-scale maps and synapse-scale EM.
ocar.challenge: Building one requires knowing cell-type composition of regions and each type’s input and output patterns—still incomplete in mammals.
ocar.action: Zeng (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2018) reviews historical and modern anterograde and retrograde tracing at population and single-cell levels, plus imaging and network analysis for mammalian mesoscale maps.
ocar.resolution: The review organizes how tracing, imaging, and graph analysis combine to map type-to-type pathways across the brain.
ocar.future_work: A complete mammalian mesoscale connectome remains a community goal the review surveys rather than finishes.

summaries.beginner: Besides whole-brain scans and synapse-level pictures, scientists also need maps of how cell types in one region talk to cell types in another. This review explains tracing methods that follow those medium-scale pathways in mammal brains.
summaries.intermediate: Zeng (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2018) reviews mesoscale connectomics: connections between neuronal types across brain regions. Building such maps requires cell-type composition plus input/output patterns. The article surveys anterograde and retrograde tracing at population and single-cell resolution, and imaging plus network analysis for mammalian brains.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. Mesoscale is explicitly distinguished from macro- and micro-connectomes. No new tracing dataset is presented. Completeness of then-current mouse mesoscale efforts is discussed in the paper body, not the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Besides whole-brain scans and synapse-level pictures, scientists also need maps of how cell types in one region talk to cell types in another. This review explains tracing methods that follow those medium-scale pathways in mammal brains.

ocar.opportunity: Linking neuron function to synaptic structure in the same animal is required for mechanistic circuit understanding; larval zebrafish are small and transparent enough that whole anatomically defined regions can be imaged both ways.
ocar.challenge: Few vertebrates allow activity of many neurons and synaptic-resolution EM of entire regions in one specimen.
ocar.action: Wanner and Vishwanathan (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2018) review combining multiphoton calcium imaging with dense EM circuit reconstruction in larval zebrafish, including required tools.
ocar.resolution: They describe practical methods to register function to synaptic wiring across entire brain regions in this vertebrate.
ocar.future_work: The review is a methods guide; executing region-complete function-plus-structure still depends on matching two huge datasets from one fish.

summaries.beginner: To know what a circuit does, it helps to watch cells fire and then see exactly how they are wired, in the same animal. Young zebrafish are small and clear enough that this is possible for whole brain regions, and this review explains how.
summaries.intermediate: Wanner and Vishwanathan (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2018) review mapping activity to synaptic connectivity in larval zebrafish. Multiphoton calcium imaging is paired with dense EM reconstruction of entire anatomically defined regions, using the larva’s small size and optical transparency. The article catalogs methods and tools rather than a new connectome.
summaries.advanced: Function–structure registration error is the central practical caveat and is not quantified here. “Entire regions” is the aspiration they argue is uniquely feasible in this vertebrate. EM density and proofreading completeness vary by study they cite.

plain_language_summary: To know what a circuit does, it helps to watch cells fire and then see exactly how they are wired, in the same animal. Young zebrafish are small and clear enough that this is possible for whole brain regions, and this review explains how.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans encodes over 300 peptides from at least 154 precursor genes, creating a wireless layer on top of wired synapses. SEB-3 is an orphan secretin-family GPCR conserved in bilaterians.
ocar.challenge: Which peptides activate SEB-3, and which behaviors it controls, were unknown.
ocar.action: Chew et al. (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2018) use reverse pharmacology to identify NLP-49 as a SEB-3 ligand and then analyze locomotion, arousal, and egg-laying in mutants and overexpression lines.
ocar.resolution: seb-3 and nlp-49 deletions cause similar locomotor-dynamics defects reversed by wild-type transgenes. NLP-49 overexpression in AVK heightens locomotor arousal in a seb-3-dependent way. Both genes affect constitutive egg-laying in liquid and similar temporal egg-laying patterns.
ocar.future_work: The work is part of a “connectome to behaviour” discussion issue; how NLP-49/SEB-3 sits on the synaptic wiring diagram is not mapped here.

summaries.beginner: Worms use small peptides as extra chemical messages beyond their wired connections. This study found a peptide and its receptor that together change how the worm crawls, how alert it is, and when it lays eggs.
summaries.intermediate: Chew et al. (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2018) identify NLP-49 peptides as ligands of the secretin GPCR SEB-3 via reverse pharmacology. Loss of either gene produces similar locomotion-dynamic defects rescued by overexpression of wild-type transgenes. AVK overexpression of NLP-49 increases locomotor arousal in a seb-3-dependent manner, and both mutants alter egg-laying in similar ways.
summaries.advanced: Ligand identification is reverse pharmacology; in vivo site of action is partly pinned to AVK for the arousal overexpression phenotype. High-content locomotion similarity is qualitative in the abstract (“remarkably similar”). This is neuromodulation, not a synaptic reconstruction. The article belongs to a C. elegans cellular-resolution modelling issue.

plain_language_summary: Worms use small peptides as extra chemical messages beyond their wired connections. This study found a peptide and its receptor that together change how the worm crawls, how alert it is, and when it lays eggs.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is a tractable model for locomotion, navigation, and decision-making in complex sensory worlds, and whole-brain plus freely moving calcium imaging now exist.
ocar.challenge: A feed-forward view in which sensory pathways converge onto premotor neurons may be wrong if even high-level interneurons are tightly locked to ongoing behavior.
ocar.action: Kaplan, Nichols, and Zimmer (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2018) synthesize imaging studies showing interneuron activity coupled to instantaneous behavior, including neurons that receive direct sensory input.
ocar.resolution: They propose distributed dynamical sensorimotor integration already at upper sensory layers, discuss implications for experiment design, and place the idea next to similar findings in flies and rodents.
ocar.future_work: The perspective outlines challenges for interpreting neural activity and designing experiments under this distributed view.

summaries.beginner: People often imagine worm brains as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. This opinion piece says new whole-brain recordings show many in-between cells already tracking the animal’s movement, so sensing and acting are mixed together.
summaries.intermediate: Kaplan, Nichols, and Zimmer (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2018) reappraise C. elegans sensorimotor integration in light of whole-brain and freely moving calcium imaging. Most interneurons, including some with direct sensory input, are tightly coupled to instantaneous behavior. They argue against sequential feed-forward sensory pathways onto premotor cells and for distributed dynamical integration, with parallels in flies and rodents.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not new data. Coupling to behavior could reflect corollary discharge, proprioception, or true mixed computation; the abstract treats the observation as a challenge to feed-forward intuition. Experimental-design implications are discussed at a high level. The piece sits in a connectome-to-behaviour theme issue.

plain_language_summary: People often imagine worm brains as a one-way path from sensors to muscles. This opinion piece says new whole-brain recordings show many in-between cells already tracking the animal’s movement, so sensing and acting are mixed together.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping synapses with EM or paired recordings is labor-intensive; a genetic reporter of contacts would speed circuit mapping in Drosophila.
ocar.challenge: Earlier GRASP methods can light up non-synaptic membrane appositions, and they were not equally usable with all three fly binary transcription systems in both directions.
ocar.action: Shearin et al. (Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 2018) target split-GFP fragments to pre- and postsynaptic proteins (t-GRASP) and test larval sensory neurons, neuromuscular junctions, and adult photoreceptors.
ocar.resolution: Pairing targeted pre- and post-t-GRASP constructs yields strong synaptic-region signal with minimal false positives. Activity-independent t-GRASP is more synapse-specific than existing fly GRASP, and stocks work with all three binary systems in either direction.
ocar.future_work: t-GRASP assesses connectivity genetically; it does not replace EM for synapse ultrastructure or counts.

summaries.beginner: To see whether two fly neurons touch at a synapse, researchers can split a fluorescent protein so it lights up only when the cells meet. This paper aims that trick more carefully at true synaptic sites and makes it work with the common fly genetic toolkits.
summaries.intermediate: Shearin et al. (Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 2018) develop t-GRASP, targeting GRASP split-GFP to pre- and postsynaptic/dendritic proteins in Drosophila. Tests in larval sensory neurons, NMJs, and adult photoreceptors show preferential synaptic-region signal and little false-positive labeling. The method is activity-independent, more synapse-specific than prior fly GRASP, and usable with all three binary transcription systems in either direction.
summaries.advanced: “Minimal false-positive signal” is relative to existing GRASP, not a measured false-discovery rate versus EM in the abstract. Activity independence means it reports contact potential, not use. NMJ and photoreceptor tests may not capture all CNS neuropil geometries.

plain_language_summary: To see whether two fly neurons touch at a synapse, researchers can split a fluorescent protein so it lights up only when the cells meet. This paper aims that trick more carefully at true synaptic sites and makes it work with the common fly genetic toolkits.

ocar.opportunity: Aging changes cortical neuropil; dense 3D EM can show how synapse loss is or is not compensated in a defined layer.
ocar.challenge: Qualitative EM can miss coordinated changes in synapse size, inhibitory fraction, and correlations among spine, bouton, and vesicle measures.
ocar.action: Calì et al. (PLoS ONE, 2018) densely reconstruct axons, dendrites, and synapses in layer 1 of mouse somatosensory cortex in aged versus adult animals.
ocar.resolution: Excitatory synapse loss is balanced by larger remaining synapses so total synaptic surface per axon length and per neuropil volume stays the same. Inhibitory synapses, especially on spines, decline more, raising E/I balance. Correlations among spine volume, bouton volume, synapse size, and docked vesicles are preserved. The pattern suggests reduced plasticity with fewer transient connections but compensation that preserves remaining connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The comparison is layer 1 somatosensory cortex; other layers and regions may age differently.

summaries.beginner: In old mice, the outer layer of touch cortex loses some connections between nerve cells, but the remaining connections get larger, so the total contact area stays about the same. Inhibitory connections shrink more than excitatory ones, and the usual size matching between sending and receiving parts of a synapse is still there.
summaries.intermediate: Calì et al. (PLoS ONE, 2018) use dense serial-EM reconstructions of mouse somatosensory layer 1 to compare aged and adult neuropil. Excitatory synapse number falls but size rises, holding synaptic surface per axon length and per volume constant. Inhibitory synapses decline more, particularly on spines, increasing E/I balance. Spine–bouton–synapse–docked-vesicle correlations persist, interpreted as reduced plasticity with compensatory strengthening.
summaries.advanced: Compensation of total synaptic surface does not imply unchanged function. E/I is a structural ratio, not measured inhibition. Age groups and n are not in the abstract. Dense reconstruction still depends on segmentation error. Causal direction (aging versus experience) is not separable here.

plain_language_summary: In old mice, the outer layer of touch cortex loses some connections between nerve cells, but the remaining connections get larger, so the total contact area stays about the same. Inhibitory connections shrink more than excitatory ones, and the usual size matching between sending and receiving parts of a synapse is still there.

ocar.opportunity: Feeding requires central circuits that convert internal and external sensory input into motor, modulatory, and endocrine output, but those paths were unmapped at synapse resolution in Drosophila larvae.
ocar.challenge: How enteric, pharyngeal, and external sensory neurons converge onto pharyngeal motor neurons, serotonergic modulators, and ring-gland neuroendocrine cells was unknown.
ocar.action: Miroschnikow et al. (bioRxiv, 2018) reconstruct the synaptic map of feeding-related inputs and outputs from a whole-CNS EM volume.
ocar.resolution: Inputs form seven distinct sensory synaptic compartments. Monosynaptic links from a subset of compartments cover motor and endocrine targets in overlapping domains; polysynaptic routes superimpose, yielding divergent sensory paths that reconverge on common outputs. A different set of compartments connects to the mushroom-body calyx.
ocar.future_work: The architecture is a reconstructed snapshot; physiological tests of which paths dominate during feeding states are not in this abstract.

summaries.beginner: Scientists traced the wiring that lets a fly maggot eat, from sense organs around the mouth to the muscles and hormone cells that carry out feeding. Signals gather in seven pockets in the brain, then split and rejoin on the way to the same motor outputs; memory circuits sit on a different set of inputs.
summaries.intermediate: Miroschnikow et al. (bioRxiv, 2018) reconstruct a Drosophila larval feeding connectome from a whole-CNS EM volume. Sensory neurons from enteric, pharyngeal, and external organs occupy seven synaptic compartments. Monosynaptic connections from some compartments overlap on pharyngeal motor, serotonergic, and ring-gland targets, with polysynaptic routes superimposed. Separate compartments feed the mushroom-body calyx.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint (later published as an eLife paper not used here). Seven compartments are defined by presynaptic-site distributions. “Cover” of outputs is anatomical, not a physiological sufficiency test. Completeness depends on the larval CNS volume and proofreading of this subgraph.

plain_language_summary: Scientists traced the wiring that lets a fly maggot eat, from sense organs around the mouth to the muscles and hormone cells that carry out feeding. Signals gather in seven pockets in the brain, then split and rejoin on the way to the same motor outputs; memory circuits sit on a different set of inputs.

ocar.opportunity: Network complexity measures can show whether a connectome is more structured than its degree sequence implies. The C. elegans somatic gap-junction network is a small, fully mapped test case.
ocar.challenge: High complexity might be concentrated in a few connections, and those connections might match independently defined “rich club” neurons from the synaptic network.
ocar.action: Kunert-Graf, Sakhanenko, and Galas (Entropy, 2017) measure complexity of the C. elegans gap-junction connectome, then progressively delete complexity-causing connections.
ocar.resolution: The network is much more complex than expected from degree distribution; excess complexity comes from a small set of command-interneuron connections. After those deletions, complexity falls below a random network. The implicated neurons match the synaptic network’s rich club.
ocar.future_work: The view of a low-complexity background plus symmetry-breaking rich-club connections is specific to this gap-junction graph; chemical synapses are a separate network.

summaries.beginner: Not all wiring diagrams are equally intricate. In the worm’s electrical-junction network, a few connections involving command cells make the whole map far more complex than a random one with the same number of links per cell.
summaries.intermediate: Kunert-Graf, Sakhanenko, and Galas (Entropy, 2017) apply a complexity measure to the C. elegans somatic gap-junction connectome. Complexity far exceeds degree-sequence expectation because of a small set of command-interneuron connections. Deleting those links drops complexity below random. The same neurons were previously identified as a synaptic-network rich club.
summaries.advanced: Complexity is a specific information-theoretic or graph measure (not named in the abstract). Gap-junction graphs omit chemical synapses by design. Progressive deletion is an in silico intervention, not a biological ablation. Alignment with the synaptic rich club is a correspondence of neuron sets, not a joint multiplex analysis in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Not all wiring diagrams are equally intricate. In the worm’s electrical-junction network, a few connections involving command cells make the whole map far more complex than a random one with the same number of links per cell.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding computations in circuits requires knowing how neurons are connected, and aberrant wiring may contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders.
ocar.challenge: Available methods for visualizing circuits have severe limitations, making precise wiring diagrams hard to extract, so new approaches keep appearing.
ocar.action: Lee, Huang, De La Cruz, Callejas, and Lois (Fly, 2017) review methods to investigate nervous-system structure and connectivity and discuss strengths and limits.
ocar.resolution: The review is a comparative methods survey rather than a new dataset, aimed at helping readers choose tools.
ocar.future_work: They emphasize that no single method currently yields complete, precise wiring from routine histology, so method choice remains question-dependent.

summaries.beginner: To figure out how a brain circuit works, you need to know who talks to whom. This short review lists ways to see those connections and honestly describes what each method can and cannot do.
summaries.intermediate: Lee et al. (Fly, 2017) review methods for investigating nervous-system structure and connectivity. They motivate the problem with the need for wiring diagrams and possible wiring defects in neurodevelopmental disorders. The article compares approaches and their limitations rather than presenting new connectivity data.
summaries.advanced: This is a concise methods review. No primary numbers. Coverage of EM versus genetic tracers versus light microscopy is in the body, not the abstract. Fly journal venue does not restrict the methods to Drosophila only as stated in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: To figure out how a brain circuit works, you need to know who talks to whom. This short review lists ways to see those connections and honestly describes what each method can and cannot do.

ocar.opportunity: Neuronal boundary detection in EM assists automatic circuit reconstruction for connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Detectors must catch both filament-thin and blob-thick membranes while ignoring ambiguous intracellular structure.
ocar.action: Shen, Wang, Jiang, Wang, and Yuille (ICCV, 2017) propose multi-stage fully convolutional networks whose later stages take multiple recursive side outputs with different receptive fields from earlier stages, trained end-to-end.
ocar.resolution: They report promising results on mouse piriform cortex and ISBI 2012 EM segmentation datasets, analogizing the multi-scale recursive inputs to comparing alternative segmentations as in human vision.
ocar.future_work: Promising results on two public sets leave larger anisotropic volumes as the obvious harder test.

summaries.beginner: Computers tracing brain cells must find membranes that can look like thin threads or thick blobs, and ignore clutter inside the cell. This team built a multi-step neural network that looks at several zoom levels at once and did well on two public electron-microscope contests.
summaries.intermediate: Shen et al. (ICCV, 2017) introduce multi-stage multi-recursive-input fully convolutional networks for neuronal boundary detection in EM. Multiple side outputs with different receptive fields from one stage feed the next as multi-scale contextual boundaries. End-to-end training yields promising results on mouse piriform cortex and ISBI 2012.
summaries.advanced: “Promising” is qualitative; scores are not in the abstract. The human-vision analogy is rhetorical. ISBI 2012 and piriform cortex were standard 2017 benchmarks, smaller than later connectomic volumes. Recursive inputs can propagate early errors as well as context.

plain_language_summary: Computers tracing brain cells must find membranes that can look like thin threads or thick blobs, and ignore clutter inside the cell. This team built a multi-step neural network that looks at several zoom levels at once and did well on two public electron-microscope contests.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila vision is numerically small enough that a complete synaptic wiring diagram of the first visual neuropil could explain a wide range of light-driven behaviors.
ocar.challenge: How two photoreceptor subtypes partition absolute intensity versus temporal change, and how local processing reaches mushroom body and lateral horn, was unmapped at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Larderet et al. (bioRxiv / eLife DOI in metadata, 2017) map the larval visual circuit’s synaptic wiring and neurotransmitters.
ocar.resolution: The two PR subtypes contact different targets, creating parallel circuits potentially for absolute intensity versus temporal change. Dedicated projection interneurons reach lateral horn and mushroom body. Stratified larval optic neuropil organization suggests common principles with adult fly and vertebrate visual systems.
ocar.future_work: They present the complete LON wiring diagram as enabling later study of how small circuits control many behaviors.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly maggots have a tiny visual system with only two kinds of light sensors. Mapping every connection showed that those two kinds feed different pathways, one perhaps for how bright it is and one for how light is changing, before signals go on to learning and other brain areas.
summaries.intermediate: Larderet et al. (2017; journal field bioRxiv) reconstruct the Drosophila larval visual circuit, including synapses and transmitters. Two photoreceptor subtypes create parallel paths potentially computing absolute intensity versus temporal change already in the first visual center. Projection interneurons then target lateral horn and mushroom body. Stratification of the larval optic neuropil is likened to adult fly and vertebrate visual systems.
summaries.advanced: Functional assignments (intensity vs change) are potential, based on different targets, not physiology in the abstract. “Complete” refers to the LON wiring they map. Journal metadata say bioRxiv while the DOI is eLife. Transmitter assignments are part of the map but not detailed here.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly maggots have a tiny visual system with only two kinds of light sensors. Mapping every connection showed that those two kinds feed different pathways, one perhaps for how bright it is and one for how light is changing, before signals go on to learning and other brain areas.

ocar.opportunity: Axon routing determines how single-neuron signals are sent across the mammalian brain, but almost no long-range projection neurons have been reconstructed in full because thin axons travel many millimeters.
ocar.challenge: Axons as thin as 100 nm arborize in targets dispersed over millimeters, beyond routine light-microscopy volumes.
ocar.action: Economo et al. (eLife, 2016) build a high-speed two-photon microscope integrated with a vibratome plus computational tools for large image volumes, and reconstruct multiple mouse motor-cortex neurons brain-wide.
ocar.resolution: The platform visualizes and reconstructs long-range axonal arbors of individual neurons across a mouse brain.
ocar.future_work: They demonstrate multiple motor-cortex neurons in one brain; atlas-scale application to many cell types is the implied extension.

summaries.beginner: A single brain cell can send a thread-like axon across much of the mouse brain, thinner than a wavelength of light. This team built a fast two-photon microscope that slices as it images, so those long axons can be followed from end to end.
summaries.intermediate: Economo et al. (eLife, 2016) present a platform for high-resolution 3D fluorescence imaging of complete tissue volumes to reconstruct long-range axons. A high-speed two-photon microscope is integrated with a vibratome and tools for large-scale image data. They reconstruct axonal arbors of multiple mouse motor-cortex neurons across one brain. Axons as thin as 100 nm spanning many millimeters motivate the design.
summaries.advanced: This is light-microscopy morphology, not synaptic EM. Completeness of “entire” arbors depends on labeling and signal-to-noise at 100 nm-scale axons. One brain and multiple motor-cortex cells constitute the demonstration. Infrastructure is the contribution.

plain_language_summary: A single brain cell can send a thread-like axon across much of the mouse brain, thinner than a wavelength of light. This team built a fast two-photon microscope that slices as it images, so those long axons can be followed from end to end.

ocar.opportunity: How genes encode synaptic connections remains unsolved; C. elegans connectivity, including complex male mating circuits, offers a search space for those genes.
ocar.challenge: Male mating networks look complex enough to need a large family of molecular labels for pre- and postsynaptic recognition.
ocar.action: Emmons (Current Topics in Developmental Biology, 2016) argues that a combinatorial code of neural cell-adhesion proteins might be found by comparing candidate-gene expression with the connection pattern.
ocar.resolution: The chapter frames connectomics as a genetics problem: expression–connectivity comparison as a path to the labeling code.
ocar.future_work: The suggested discovery strategy is prospective; the chapter does not report the code itself.

summaries.beginner: We still do not know how DNA tells nerve cells which partners to connect with. This essay says the worm, especially the male’s mating circuits, is a good place to hunt for the molecular name tags that might form a combinatorial connection code.
summaries.intermediate: Emmons (Current Topics in Developmental Biology, 2016) discusses genetic encoding of synapses using C. elegans, including male mating circuits as a complex network that may require many molecular labels. He proposes discovering a combinatorial cell-adhesion code by matching candidate-gene expression patterns to connectivity. The piece is a perspective, not a new connectome.
summaries.advanced: The “large family of labels” need is an argument from circuit complexity, not a counted lower bound in the abstract. Combinatorial adhesion is a hypothesis. Male mating connectome details are assumed known from prior reconstructions.

plain_language_summary: We still do not know how DNA tells nerve cells which partners to connect with. This essay says the worm, especially the male’s mating circuits, is a good place to hunt for the molecular name tags that might form a combinatorial connection code.

ocar.opportunity: Array tomography can put fluorescence on serial EM sections, but super-resolution on the same section would better identify electrical synapses in the C. elegans connectome.
ocar.challenge: Correlating molecular labels with ultrastructure at high confidence remains difficult, especially for gap junctions.
ocar.action: Markert et al. (Neurophotonics, 2016) combine high-pressure freezing and freeze substitution with array tomography plus SIM or dSTORM and SEM on the same section, correlating via endogenous landmarks.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate precise, unbiased correlation sufficient to identify and label C. elegans gap junctions, and they argue even smaller structures are feasible—filling a molecular gap in connectomes that otherwise miss electrical-synapse identity.
ocar.future_work: The method is shown for gap junctions; broader molecular inventory of the worm connectome would apply the same correlation pipeline.

summaries.beginner: Ordinary wiring maps often miss or cannot name electrical synapses. These researchers lined up super-resolution light pictures with electron-microscope pictures of the same worm sections so they could both see and molecularly tag those electrical junctions.
summaries.intermediate: Markert et al. (Neurophotonics, 2016) add super-resolution (SIM and dSTORM) to array tomography on high-pressure-frozen C. elegans sections, then SEM of the same section. Correlation uses endogenous landmarks and open image software. They identify and label gap junctions with high confidence, aiming to add molecular identity of electrical synapses to the connectome.
summaries.advanced: “Unbiased” correlation via landmarks still has a residual registration error not quantified in the abstract. High-pressure freezing aids near-native preservation but is not artifact-free. Gap-junction identification is the demonstrated use case. Throughput versus whole-nervous-system coverage is not claimed.

plain_language_summary: Ordinary wiring maps often miss or cannot name electrical synapses. These researchers lined up super-resolution light pictures with electron-microscope pictures of the same worm sections so they could both see and molecularly tag those electrical junctions.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uses gap junctions in virtually all cells, with a surprisingly large innexin gene family, making it a model for electrical-synapse roles in behavior and development.
ocar.challenge: Many cell types express multiple innexins, so redundancy limits single-gene knockdown phenotypes and obscures which junctions do what.
ocar.action: Hall (Developmental Neurobiology, 2016) reviews general properties of nematode gap junctions, expression patterns, and known roles in development and the connectome.
ocar.resolution: The review summarizes how diverse junction types arise from multiple innexins and what is known about their behavioral and developmental jobs.
ocar.future_work: Redundancy implies that multi-innexin genetics and better molecular identification of junctions in the connectome remain necessary.

summaries.beginner: The worm uses electrical bridges between cells almost everywhere, and it has many genes for the proteins that make those bridges. This review explains what those bridges do in development and behavior, and why knocking out just one gene often barely matters.
summaries.intermediate: Hall (Developmental Neurobiology, 2016) reviews C. elegans gap junctions (innexins) across tissues. A large innexin family and co-expression of multiple innexins create diverse junctions and mute single-gene phenotypes. The review covers expression, developmental and behavioral roles, and place in the connectome.
summaries.advanced: This is a review (2016, with 2017 pagination noted). No new connectome. Redundancy is the central genetic caveat. Electrical versus chemical contributions to behavior must be read from the cited literature.

plain_language_summary: The worm uses electrical bridges between cells almost everywhere, and it has many genes for the proteins that make those bridges. This review explains what those bridges do in development and behavior, and why knocking out just one gene often barely matters.

ocar.opportunity: Twelve macaque bipolar types have been described morphologically; type-specific synaptic rules, especially ON versus OFF counterparts, still needed serial EM in rod-dense perifovea.
ocar.challenge: Assigning each ON type a counterpart among OFF types, and tracing where S-cone signals go, requires a complete local SSTEM census.
ocar.action: Tsukamoto and Omi (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2016) use serial-section TEM in macaque perifovea to reconfirm ON bipolar classes (IMB, DB4–6, GB, BB) and quantify their synapses.
ocar.resolution: They propose ON/OFF counterparts (IMB/BB with FMB; DB4 with DB2; DB5 with DB3a; DB6 with DB1; GB with DB3b). GB contacts rods and cones like DB3b, a candidate substrate for fast mesopic rod signals. Two-step connections largely confine S-cone output to small bistratified and some OFF midget ganglion cells, while other midget and parasol paths are M/L-dominant.
ocar.future_work: Perifoveal rod-dense tissue may not match foveal cone-pure circuitry; that eccentricity caveat is implicit in the sampling.

summaries.beginner: The monkey retina has many kinds of bipolar cells that split cone signals into ON and OFF streams. By reconstructing them in serial electron-microscope sections, this study matches each ON type to an OFF partner and shows how blue-cone signals are mostly funneled to a few ganglion-cell types.
summaries.intermediate: Tsukamoto and Omi (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2016) reconstruct macaque perifoveal ON bipolar cells with SSTEM. They confirm IMB, DB4, DB5, DB6, GB, and BB types and map type-specific synapses. GB contacts rods and cones, paralleling OFF DB3b, a possible basis for fast mesopic rod signals. DB6 sends 70% of ribbon contacts to ON midget ganglion cells (OFF DB1 sends 60% to OFF midgets). S-cone signals are largely restricted to small bistratified and some OFF midget ganglion cells.
summaries.advanced: Percentages (70%, 60%) are ribbon-contact fractions for DB6/DB1 in this perifoveal sample. Counterpart pairings are morphological/synaptic analogies. Fast mesopic rod signals are a psychophysics link, not a recording from GB cells here. Catalog mouse-retina tags do not match macaque.

plain_language_summary: The monkey retina has many kinds of bipolar cells that split cone signals into ON and OFF streams. By reconstructing them in serial electron-microscope sections, this study matches each ON type to an OFF partner and shows how blue-cone signals are mostly funneled to a few ganglion-cell types.

ocar.opportunity: X-rays can image thick brain samples in 3D without sectioning, offering faster mesoscale maps than slice-and-stain light or EM.
ocar.challenge: Quantifying cells, vessels, and myelinated axons from synchrotron microtomography still needs sample prep, segmentation, and statistics pipelines.
ocar.action: Dyer et al. (eNeuro, 2016) demonstrate synchrotron µCT at about 1 µm³ resolution on millimeter-scale mouse-brain volumes, with automated segmentation of cells, blood vessels, and myelinated axons.
ocar.resolution: They show rapid quantification of large volumes as a complement to other mapping and connectomics methods, not a replacement for synaptic EM.
ocar.future_work: Mesoscale (~1 µm³) cannot resolve synapses; combining µCT with EM or tracing is left as complementary use.

summaries.beginner: Instead of slicing a brain into thousands of slivers, these researchers used powerful X-rays to see inside millimeter-sized pieces of mouse brain in 3D. At about a micron resolution they could count cells, blood vessels, and insulated fibers quickly.
summaries.intermediate: Dyer et al. (eNeuro, 2016) use synchrotron X-ray microtomography to produce mesoscale (~1 µm³) maps from millimeter-scale mouse-brain volumes without sectioning. A pipeline covers preparation, imaging, and automated segmentation of cells, vessels, and myelinated axons, plus statistical analyses. They present µCT as rapid large-volume quantification complementary to connectomics.
summaries.advanced: Resolution is mesoscale, not synaptic. Automated segmentation accuracy is not scored in the abstract. Millimeter-scale FOV is much smaller than a whole mouse brain. Synchrotron access is a practical limit.

plain_language_summary: Instead of slicing a brain into thousands of slivers, these researchers used powerful X-rays to see inside millimeter-sized pieces of mouse brain in 3D. At about a micron resolution they could count cells, blood vessels, and insulated fibers quickly.

ocar.opportunity: Direction-selective signaling in starburst amacrine-cell dendrites is central to retinal motion detection, but intrinsic versus network contributions remain unclear, and mouse versus rabbit wiring may differ.
ocar.challenge: Synapse distributions along SAC dendrites had not been fully reconstructed in mouse, so models often borrowed rabbit connectivity.
ocar.action: Ding, Smith, Poleg-Polsky, Diamond, and Briggman (Nature, 2016) reconstruct mouse SAC circuitry connectomically and build an anatomically constrained network model, then test predictions with dendritic calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: Inputs are restricted to proximal dendrites (segregated from outputs). Inhibitory-input distribution differs fundamentally from rabbit. The model indicates mouse SAC–SAC wiring supports lower linear velocities matching smaller eye diameter, conserving angular-velocity tuning—confirmed by calcium imaging.
ocar.future_work: Species-specific wiring is shown for SACs; whether other retinal computations show similar eye-size scaling is not addressed.

summaries.beginner: Some cells in the eye are wired to notice which way things move. Mapping those cells in the mouse showed that their connection pattern is not the same as in the rabbit, and a model plus imaging suggest the mouse wiring is tuned to slower real-world speeds that match its smaller eye.
